When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

issues.explanation: For a witnessed-other-trauma profile, 'being seen' and 'being criticised or corrected' are hard to reconcile as primary trauma triggers unless the witnessed event specifically involved scrutiny or humiliation; nothing else in the profile supports that context.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected

'Time of day the event occurred' links well with hypervigilance to sounds, but 'being seen' and 'being criticised' do not connect clearly to the selected threat items.

# Clinical Vignette: Karim

Karim is a forty-one-year-old man of Lebanese descent who has worked the morning shift at a fast-food restaurant in the suburbs of Columbus, Ohio for the past six years. He lives alone in a studio apartment three blocks from the restaurant, a proximity that once felt convenient but has come to define the narrow geography of his life. He came to his first appointment with a PCL-5 score of 64, describing himself as "trapped" and "waiting for something bad to happen." The words came slowly, as if he were translating from another language, though English is his first language. He seemed to be translating from a different internal state entirely.

Three years ago, Karim witnessed a fatal shooting at a convenience store where he had stopped to buy coffee before his shift. It was 5:47 in the morning—the store was nearly empty. A man in a dark jacket entered, argued with the clerk about a price, and within seconds produced a gun. The clerk, a woman in her sixties whose name was Diane, was shot once in the chest. Karim watched her fall. He remembered the specific sound—not the gunshot itself, which was louder than anything he had ever heard, but the sound of her body hitting the floor. He remembered the smell. He remembered that the shooter had looked directly at him for what felt like an eternity but was probably two seconds, then turned and left. Karim had not been harmed. Diane had died at the scene.

In the weeks following, Karim found that 5:47 a.m. had become a time of unbearable dread. He would wake at 5:30, his body rigid, waiting for that minute to pass. He began arriving at work earlier, then earlier still, trying to move past the threshold before his body's internal clock reached that moment. Within two months, he had stopped leaving his apartment before dawn. He requested a shift change to afternoons, then evenings. His manager, a man named Derek, had been understanding at first, but after six weeks of shift shuffling and Karim's increasing unreliability, Derek had pulled him aside and told him he needed to "get it together" and "stop making excuses." The criticism—delivered in front of two coworkers during a lunch rush—had sent Karim into a state of panic so acute he had left the restaurant and not returned for three days.

He had come to believe that criticism of any kind was a sign that others could see his weakness, that they knew he was broken. When his supervisor corrected his order-taking procedure last month, Karim had felt certain the man was assessing him for some fundamental failure. The thought had spiraled: if Derek noticed something was wrong, others would too. The shame of being seen as damaged had become almost as frightening as the trauma itself.

Karim's sense of safety had contracted to almost nothing. He felt secure only in his apartment, and even then, only in his bedroom with the door locked and music playing softly—something to mask unexpected sounds. Loud noises sent him into a state of acute vigilance. A car horn, a motorcycle passing on the street, the neighbor's dog barking—each sound triggered an immediate scan of his body for injury, a frantic mental calculation of threat. He had come to understand the world as a place where violence could erupt without warning, where the ordinary moment could turn catastrophic in the space of a breath.

Over the past year, his world had contracted further. He had stopped accepting invitations from his cousin. He had quit his job three weeks ago after becoming convinced that a delay in a delivery—the supplier was running forty minutes behind schedule—meant something catastrophic had happened, that chaos was unfolding somewhere and would soon reach him. He had left work mid-shift, certain that waiting for the delivery to arrive was itself a sign of impending danger. His cousin had called repeatedly, asking if he was okay, and Karim had told him he was fine, that he just needed time. But the truth was that Karim was now unemployed, increasingly isolated, and spending most of his time in his apartment, waiting for 5:47 a.m. to arrive and pass, then waiting for the next one.

He had finally called a therapist's office this week because he had realized, with a kind of hollow clarity, that he was no longer living—he was simply existing in the space between moments of terror, hoping that one day the fear would somehow exhaust itself and leave him alone.
